props.title: The Secret of Kells
props.initialSlug: Young monk's quest weaves Celtic art & magic

sections.content: The Secret of Kells revolutionized animated storytelling by fusing medieval Celtic art with contemporary animation techniques. Drawing direct inspiration from the illuminated Book of Kells, directors Tomm Moore and Nora Twomey created a visual feast that stands apart from both Western and Eastern animation traditions. The film's distinctive angular character designs and intricate spiral patterns echo actual medieval manuscripts, while its use of flattened perspective and geometric shapes recalls the work of Gustav Klimt and early Christian iconography.

movies.title: Song of the Sea
movies.slug: Moore's spiritual successor to Kells, weaving Irish selkie mythology into a touching story about loss and family

sections.content: This film kicked off a remarkable renaissance in European animation focused on cultural preservation. Song of the Sea (2014) and Wolfwalkers (2020) completed Moore's informal "Irish Folklore Trilogy," each building on Kells' distinctive visual language while exploring Celtic mythology. Meanwhile, Tales of the Night (2011) by Michel Ocelot used shadow puppet aesthetics to adapt folk tales, demonstrating how traditional art forms could inspire innovative animation approaches.

The film's themes of knowledge preservation during times of conflict mirror similar concerns in The Name of the Rose (1986) and Fahrenheit 451 (1966). However, Kells takes a uniquely optimistic stance, celebrating the power of art and imagination to preserve culture. This contrasts sharply with the more dystopian The Black Cauldron (1985), Disney's darker take on Celtic mythology. SUBHEAD: Impact on Contemporary Animation

movies.title: Wolfwalkers
movies.slug: The stunning conclusion to Moore's Irish folklore trilogy, following a young apprentice hunter in 17th century Ireland

sections.content: The Secret of Kells helped spark a movement away from 3D computer animation dominance. Films like Ernest & Celestine (2012) and The Tale of the Princess Kaguya (2013) similarly embraced distinctive 2D styles rooted in cultural artistic traditions. This influence extends to recent works like Klaus (2019), which combines traditional animation techniques with innovative lighting effects.
